steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on rewriting and inductive reasoning. It should explain how induction is built into saturation-based theorem proving, why this clashes with how superposition works, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Background: automating induction; induction in saturation-based theorem proving
2. Form of the induction rules and how they are triggered
3. Challenge: triggered induction vs. efficient superposition
4. Our contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- automating proof by induction: particularly hard, long history
- recent promising line: integrate induction into saturation-based first-order theorem proving
- extend logical calculus with induction inference rules

2. Induction rules
- form: \neg L[t]\lor C \mathsf{cnf}(\neg F\lor C)
- \neg L[t]\lor C clause, \neg L[t] ground literal, t term of inductive data type
- F\to\forall x.L[x] instance of valid second-order induction schema, e.g. structural induction
- schema instance resolves \neg L[t] but never added to search space -> conclusion derived via inductive reasoning
- rule triggered by presence of \neg L[t] in search space; no such literal -> no induction
- only premises of schema instances directly related to a selected clause are added
- strong heuristic, esp. with full first-order logic and theories

3. Challenge: tension between two competing factors
- (i) valid goal may need a certain consequence C, which triggers induction rule with premise C with a specific schema
- (ii) efficient calculi (superposition) derive/retain only consequences absolutely required for completeness -> rule for missing C might not be applied
- motivating example (Section 0.2): lost proof in practice

4. Contributions
- counter-intuitive: derive slightly more consequences than usual to trigger induction rules with suitable schemas; as few extra as possible to keep first-order efficiency
- motivated by program verification; focus on unit-equational fragment of first-order logic with induction
- (1) modified superposition calculus with slightly relaxed constraints (Section 0.4)
- (2) new restrictions for efficiency, keeping ability to generate consequences (Section 0.4)
- (3) better redundancy elimination: sufficient conditions for skipping redundant induction steps and rewrites (Section 0.5)
- (4) implementation in Vampire, applied to inductive properties (Section 0.6); improves state of the art

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Automating proofs by induction is a hard task, and people have been working on it for a long time. One recent line of research that looks promising is to integrate induction into saturation-based first-order theorem proving, which is done by extending the logical calculus with induction inference rules. These induction rules have the following form

\neg L[t]\lor C \mathsf{cnf}(\neg F\lor C)

where \neg L[t]\lor C is a clause, \neg L[t] is a ground literal, t is a term of some inductive data type, and F\to\forall x.L[x] is an instance of some valid second-order induction schema, for example structural induction. The schema instance F\to\forall x.L[x] is used to resolve \neg L[t], but the schema instance itself is never added to the saturation search space, and this makes sure that the conclusion of the inference is derived by inductive reasoning. So the induction rule is applied only when it is triggered by the literal \neg L[t] being in the search space. If there is no such literal, then no induction is applied. Because induction is only applied when it is triggered, only premises of schema instances that are directly related to a clause selected during proof search get added to the search space. This is a strong heuristic for automating induction, especially when there is full first-order logic and theories.

## Challenge.

The problem is that applying induction only when it is triggered creates a tension between two factors that compete with each other:

- (i) A valid goal might not be provable unless a certain consequence C is derived, and this C in turn triggers an induction rule with premise C with a specific schema.

- (ii) Efficient first-order calculi like superposition try very hard to derive and keep only the consequences that are absolutely required for completeness. So induction rules that could be triggered by a consequence C which is missing might not be applied.

In our motivating example (Section 0.2) we show that this tension causes a proof to be lost in practice, since superposition may avoid generating consequences that would be needed in inductive proofs.

## Our contributions.

- counter-intuitive for superposition people: derive slightly more consequences than usual to trigger induction rules with suitable schemas
- but as few extra consequences as possible -> keep high first-order efficiency
- motivated by program verification; focus on unit-equational fragment of first-order logic with induction
- (1) modified superposition calculus, slightly relaxed constraints (Section 0.4) -> consequences standard superposition can't derive
- (2) new restrictions on the calculus for efficiency, keeping ability to generate consequences (Section 0.4)
- (3) improved redundancy elimination: sufficient conditions for skipping redundant induction steps and rewrites (Section 0.5)
- (4) implemented in Vampire, applied to proving inductive properties (Section 0.6); improves state of the art

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Automating proofs by induction is a hard task, and people have been working on it for a long time. One recent line of research that looks promising is to integrate induction into saturation-based first-order theorem proving, which is done by extending the logical calculus with induction inference rules. These induction rules have the following form

\neg L[t]\lor C \mathsf{cnf}(\neg F\lor C)

where \neg L[t]\lor C is a clause, \neg L[t] is a ground literal, t is a term of some inductive data type, and F\to\forall x.L[x] is an instance of some valid second-order induction schema, for example structural induction. The schema instance F\to\forall x.L[x] is used to resolve \neg L[t], but the schema instance itself is never added to the saturation search space, and this makes sure that the conclusion of the inference is derived by inductive reasoning. So the induction rule is applied only when it is triggered by the literal \neg L[t] being in the search space. If there is no such literal, then no induction is applied. Because induction is only applied when it is triggered, only premises of schema instances that are directly related to a clause selected during proof search get added to the search space. This is a strong heuristic for automating induction, especially when there is full first-order logic and theories.

## Challenge.

The problem is that applying induction only when it is triggered creates a tension between two factors that compete with each other:

- (i) A valid goal might not be provable unless a certain consequence C is derived, and this C in turn triggers an induction rule with premise C with a specific schema.

- (ii) Efficient first-order calculi like superposition try very hard to derive and keep only the consequences that are absolutely required for completeness. So induction rules that could be triggered by a consequence C which is missing might not be applied.

In our motivating example (Section 0.2) we show that this tension causes a proof to be lost in practice, since superposition may avoid generating consequences that would be needed in inductive proofs.

## Our contributions.

So for automating (triggered) induction in saturation we have to do something that is counter-intuitive for people used to first-order superposition reasoning. We propose to derive slightly more consequences than usual, so that induction rules with suitable schemas get triggered. Of course these extra consequences must still be as few as possible, so that we keep a high level of first-order efficiency. Our motivation comes from applications in program verification, and in this paper we focus on the unit-equational fragment of first-order logic with induction. We make the following contributions.

- (1) We introduce a modified superposition calculus with slightly relaxed constraints (Section 0.4), which lets us derive consequences that standard superposition cannot derive.

- (2) We put new restrictions on our calculus (Section 0.4) to improve efficiency further while keeping our new ability to generate consequences.

- (3) We improve redundancy elimination for saturation with induction, giving sufficient conditions for when redundant induction steps and rewrites can be skipped (Section 0.5).

- (4) We implement our approach in the Vampire first-order prover and use it to prove inductive properties (Section 0.6). The results show that our work improves the state of the art in automating proofs by induction.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Automating proof by induction is a particularly hard task with a long history [1,2,3,4,5]. A recent promising line of research in this direction is the integration of induction into saturation-based first-order theorem proving [6,7], by extending the logical calculus with induction inference rules. Such induction rules are of the form

\neg L[t]\lor C \mathsf{cnf}(\neg F\lor C)

where \neg L[t]\lor C is a clause, \neg L[t] a ground literal, t a term of some inductive data type, and F\to\forall x.L[x] is an instance of some valid second-order induction schema, for example structural induction. Note that the schema instance F\to\forall x.L[x] is applied to resolve \neg L[t], but it is never added to the saturation search space, which makes sure that the conclusion of the inference is derived via inductive reasoning. The application of the induction rule is therefore triggered by the presence of the literal \neg L[t] in the search space; if there is no such literal, no induction is applied. Applying induction only when triggered means that only premises of schema instances directly related to a clause selected during proof search are added to the search space. This is a strong heuristic for automating induction, particularly in the presence of full first-order logic and theories [8,9,10].

## Challenge.

Unfortunately, applying induction only when triggered leads to a tension between two competing factors:

- (i) It may be that a valid goal is not provable without deriving a certain consequence C, which in turn triggers an induction rule with premise C with a specific schema.

- (ii) Efficient first-order calculi, such as superposition [11], go to great lengths to derive and retain only the consequences absolutely required for completeness. Therefore, induction rules that could be triggered by a (missing) consequence C might not be applied.

Our motivating example (Section 0.2) shows that this tension causes a lost proof in practice, as superposition may avoid generating consequences that would be needed in inductive proofs.

## Our contributions.

For automating (triggered) induction in saturation, we thus need to do something counter-intuitive for those used to first-order superposition reasoning. We propose deriving slightly more consequences than usual in order to trigger induction rules with suitable schemas. Naturally, this must still be as few extra consequences as possible, in order to retain a high level of first-order efficiency. Motivated by applications of program verification [12], in this paper we focus on the unit-equational fragment of first-order logic with induction and make the following contributions.

- (1) We introduce a modified superposition calculus (Section 0.4) with slightly relaxed constraints, allowing us to derive consequences that cannot be derived by standard superposition.

- (2) We impose new restrictions on our calculus (Section 0.4) to further improve efficiency while retaining our new ability to generate consequences.

- (3) We improve redundancy elimination for saturation with induction, providing sufficient conditions for skipping redundant induction steps and rewrites (Section 0.5).

- (4) We implement our approach in the Vampire first-order prover [13] and apply it to proving inductive properties (Section 0.6). Results show that our work improves the state of the art in automating proofs by induction.
